summary: Extends the RTP profile with RTCP-based feedback. Base RTCP gives only slow statistics, so this adds mechanisms for receivers to send timely feedback, such as reports of lost data, to the sender. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP/AVPF lets a receiver report a media problem sooner than a regular RTCP report would. The receiver checks whether someone else has already reported the same problem, which limits duplicate feedback.

questions: what is a generic nack in rtcp
subtitle: Adds timely receiver feedback to RTP while keeping RTCP within its bandwidth limits.

tldr.problem: Regular RTCP reports describe reception over longer periods, so they may arrive too late to help repair a particular media loss.
tldr.mechanism: The AVPF profile adds earlier RTCP feedback. Receivers delay reports by a short random interval in multiparty sessions and suppress feedback already sent by another receiver.
tldr.outcome: The profile supports targeted repair and adaptation while retaining the RTCP bandwidth constraints. RFC 4585 has been updated by RFC 5506 and RFC 8108.

today: RFC 4585 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5506 and RFC 8108. It defines the RTP/AVPF profile and its RTCP feedback rules.

sections.title: Why RTP Needs Earlier Feedback
sections.content:
RTP receivers send RTCP reports that help a sender adjust to reception quality over time. Those reports generally work over periods of seconds to minutes, which can be too slow when a sender could repair a loss while the media is still useful.

RFC 4585 defines AVPF, an extension to the Audio-visual Profile (AVP). It adds timing rules for earlier RTCP feedback and defines general and codec-specific feedback formats, while retaining the AVP bandwidth constraints for RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular RTCP reports may arrive too late to help with a specific media loss. AVPF adds a way to report such events sooner while limiting feedback traffic.

sections.title: Three Feedback Modes
sections.content:
The RFC describes Immediate Feedback, Early RTCP, and Regular RTCP modes. These names describe whether receivers can report events in time on average; they do not select a different scheduling algorithm, and participants do not need to agree on the exact boundaries.

In Immediate Feedback mode, each receiver can usually report each event with an early RTCP packet. In Early RTCP mode, not every event can be reported, but reports can still arrive often enough to help a sender adapt. In Regular RTCP mode, sending feedback about individual events is no longer useful, so the regular schedule applies.
sections.plainLanguage: Small groups may report each event quickly. Larger groups can report less often, and very large groups use regular RTCP timing.

sections.title: Scheduling and Suppressing Early Reports
sections.content:
A receiver that notices an event first checks whether a feedback packet is already scheduled and adds its report there when possible. Otherwise, a point-to-point session uses no added random delay; a multiparty session chooses a random delay up to half the regular RTCP interval.

During that delay, the receiver watches feedback from other participants. If another report covers the same information, it suppresses its own. The receiver stores observed feedback for at least two seconds to support this check.

After sending early feedback, the receiver delays its next regular report so that short-term RTCP bandwidth does not exceed the amount used without early feedback. RTCP feedback alone is not fast enough for congestion control; in a best-effort network, a TCP-friendly rate-control algorithm is required to set the media rate.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver waits briefly in a group, listens for a matching report, and stays quiet if the problem is already covered. After reporting early, it waits longer before its next regular report.

sections.title: The Shared Feedback Packet
sections.content:
Each feedback packet identifies the sender and the media source it concerns. It also carries a feedback format value, an RTCP packet type, a length, and variable feedback control information.

The transport feedback packet type is RTPFB, value 205. The payload-specific feedback packet type is PSFB, value 206. A packet can carry one or more feedback messages in its control information when that message format permits it.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared packet format says who sent feedback and which media source it concerns. A type value tells the receiver whether the information is general transport feedback or tied to a media payload.

sections.title: Generic NACK and Video Feedback
sections.content:
A Generic Negative Acknowledgement (NACK) identifies lost RTP packets with a packet identifier (PID) and a bitmask of following lost packets (BLP). PID is an RTP sequence number. The bitmask covers the next sixteen packets; a set bit reports a loss, but an unset bit does not prove the packet arrived.

Video feedback includes Picture Loss Indication, Slice Loss Indication, and Reference Picture Selection Indication. These tell an encoder about lost picture data, lost macroblocks, or a usable earlier reference picture. The application-layer feedback format carries receiver-to-sender data that the application itself must identify.

Feedback capabilities are signaled with the media-level SDP a=rtcp-fb attribute. A receiver must not use feedback types that were not listed for the session, and a sender is not required to react to a report.
sections.plainLanguage: A NACK names a missing packet and can mark losses among the next packets. Video feedback can describe damaged picture data or identify an earlier picture that the encoder can use.

sections.title: Security and Mixed Profiles
sections.content:
AVPF does not add security services beyond RTP and RTP/AVP. Earlier and more frequent reports create ways for a participant to consume RTCP bandwidth, send misleading loss reports, or make receivers suppress useful feedback.

Authenticating RTCP messages can prevent false packets from unauthenticated sources. Group authentication does not prevent a malicious or malfunctioning participant that has the group key from sending disruptive reports. Implementations should respond conservatively to unusual feedback.

AVP and AVPF participants can share a session without disrupting each other's basic operation, but AVP senders ignore AVPF feedback. An AVPF sender therefore receives feedback only from AVPF receivers, and early reports should be sent only when all senders support AVPF.
sections.plainLanguage: False or excessive reports can use bandwidth and make useful feedback less effective. Authentication can block outsiders, but it cannot stop a group member with valid credentials from misbehaving.

viz.caption: WHAT THE AVPF FEEDBACK MODES ALLOW
